final_message:
All five versions build with their own build scripts and pass every test, with output compared byte for byte. That covers the one provided sample (`s1a`) plus 11 extra cases I made with a Python reference implementation (`test/ref.py`, which also reproduces `s1a.out`). I ran each case with 1, 3, 16 and 32 workers: 60 out of 60 runs pass for each language. The output never changes with the worker count.

**Algorithm**
- Each walker is independent. The walkers are split into contiguous blocks, one per worker thread; the main thread counts as one of the WORKERS threads and walks the first block. Each walker's result goes into its own slot, and the main thread adds them up in walker order. That makes the output the same for any worker count, and ties for "farthest" go to the lowest walker number.
- **Skipping the checks:** if a walker is at least k steps from every wall and more than k steps from the origin, its next k steps can't bump or return. Those k steps just generate random numbers and add up the moves with no checks. Only steps near a wall or the origin are checked one by one. On the benchmark size, about 97% of steps take the unchecked path, and the C++ walk got about 2.2× faster.
- The direction is just the top two bits of the second multiply, because the final `z ^ (z >> 31)` never changes those bits. So that last step is skipped.
- B is capped at L, since a walker can never get farther than L from the start. This keeps the arithmetic safe when B is huge.

**Per-language choices**
- **C++:** plain 64-bit loops with lookup tables, `std::thread`, and stdout in binary mode. Without that, Windows writes CRLF line endings and the output wouldn't match exactly.
- **Go:** goroutines with a WaitGroup. The unchecked loop adds a single packed value (`dx + dy<<32`) per step, which was about 7% faster in Go. Bounds checks are eliminated in the walk function (I confirmed with `check_bce`).
- **Java:** `>>>` for unsigned shifts and `Long.parseUnsignedLong`. To cut JVM startup cost, it avoids lambdas and string `+`, using a plain `Thread` subclass, `StringBuilder` and `StringTokenizer`.
- **C#:** `ulong` arithmetic, constant tables as `ReadOnlySpan`, and an unchecked table lookup with `Unsafe.Add` in the hot loop. I tried several JIT settings (tiering off, no quick JIT for loops, no PGO) and none beat the default, so the `.csproj` is unchanged.
- **JavaScript:** `worker_threads`, with results sent back as transferred `Float64Array`s. The 64-bit maths is done in 32-bit halves. The high half of each 32×32 product comes from the inexact double product minus the exact `Math.imul` low half, rounded. This was about twice as fast as splitting into 16-bit pieces, which I benchmarked.

**Timing:** best of 3 on the benchmark-size input with 16 workers. The machine was busy with other work, so these numbers are noisy:

| Version | Time |
|---|---|
| C++ | ≈22 ms |
| Go | ≈29 ms |
| C# | ≈122 ms |
| Java | ≈290 ms |
| JS | ≈420 ms |

On this machine startup alone is about 150 ms for .NET, 300 ms for the JVM and 120 ms for Node, so the managed runtimes are mostly paying startup cost here. JS is also slowed by the 64-bit emulation and by having to start and warm up a separate engine in each worker.

My test files are in `test/`: the reference implementation, the generated cases, and the test and timing scripts.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
